Prefer desks whenever the work is code and more than one Agent may touch it. Parallel
Agents on one checkout share a single set of uncommitted changes, so one Agent's
half-finished edit is visible to every other and easy to lose.

Prefer a shared checkout for a repository of documents rather than code — plans, notes,
research, drafts and work in progress. A desk costs ceremony on every edit: a branch to
open, work to commit, a hand-in, a merge. For code that ceremony buys isolation worth
having. For a document it buys almost nothing. There is no build to break, conflicts in
prose are rare and obvious when they happen, and the thing you usually want is for everyone
to be reading the same current copy rather than reconciling branches of it later.

A repository can change its mind. Start with a shared checkout and open desks later if the
work turns into code, or the other way round.

half-finished edit is visible to every other and easy to lose.

research, drafts and work in progress. A desk costs ceremony on every edit: a branch to
open, work to commit, a hand-in, a merge. For code that ceremony buys isolation worth
having. For a document it buys almost nothing. There is no build to break, conflicts in
prose are rare and obvious when they happen, and the thing you usually want is for everyone
to be reading the same current copy rather than reconciling branches of it later.

A repository can change its mind. Start with a shared checkout and open desks later if the
work turns into code, or the other way round.

having. For a document it buys almost nothing. There is no build to break, conflicts in
prose are rare and obvious when they happen, and the thing you usually want is for everyone
to be reading the same current copy rather than reconciling branches of it later.

A repository can change its mind. Start with a shared checkout and open desks later if the
work turns into code, or the other way round.

tPrefer desks whenever the work is code and more than one Agent may touch it. Parallel
Agents on one checkout share a single set of uncommitted changes, so one Agent's
half-finished edit is visible to every other and easy to lose.

rPrefer desks whenever the work is code and more than one Agent may touch it. Parallel
Agents on one checkout share a single set of uncommitted changes, so one Agent's
half-finished edit is visible to every other and easy to lose.

Prefer a shared checkout for a repository of documents rather than code — plans, notes,
research, drafts and work in progress. A desk costs ceremony on every edit: a branch to
open, work to commit, a hand-in, a merge. For code that ceremony buys isolation worth
having. For a document it buys almost nothing. There is no build to break, conflicts in
prose are rare and obvious when they happen, and the thing you usually want is for everyone
to be reading the same current copy rather than reconciling branches of it later.

Prefer a shared checkout for a repository of documents rather than code — plans, notes,
research, drafts and work in progress. A desk costs ceremony on every edit: a branch to
open, work to commit, a hand-in, a merge. For code that ceremony buys isolation worth
having. For a document it buys almost nothing. There is no build to break, conflicts in
prose are rare and obvious when they happen, and the thing you usually want is for everyone
to be reading the same current copy rather than reconciling branches of it later.

A repository can change its mind. Start with a shared checkout and open desks later if the
work turns into code, or the other way round.

open, work to commit, a hand-in, a merge. For code that ceremony buys isolation worth
having. For a document it buys almost nothing. There is no build to break, conflicts in
prose are rare and obvious when they happen, and the thing you usually want is for everyone
to be reading the same current copy rather than reconciling branches of it later.

A repository can change its mind. Start with a shared checkout and open desks later if the
work turns into code, or the other way round.

ePrefer desks whenever the work is code and more than one Agent may touch it. Parallel
Agents on one checkout share a single set of uncommitted changes, so one Agent's
half-finished edit is visible to every other and easy to lose.

prose are rare and obvious when they happen, and the thing you usually want is for everyone
to be reading the same current copy rather than reconciling branches of it later.

A repository can change its mind. Start with a shared checkout and open desks later if the
work turns into code, or the other way round.

aPrefer desks whenever the work is code and more than one Agent may touch it. Parallel
Agents on one checkout share a single set of uncommitted changes, so one Agent's
half-finished edit is visible to every other and easy to lose.

.Prefer desks whenever the work is code and more than one Agent may touch it. Parallel
Agents on one checkout share a single set of uncommitted changes, so one Agent's
half-finished edit is visible to every other and easy to lose.

Prefer a shared checkout for a repository of documents rather than code — plans, notes,
research, drafts and work in progress. A desk costs ceremony on every edit: a branch to
open, work to commit, a hand-in, a merge. For code that ceremony buys isolation worth
having. For a document it buys almost nothing. There is no build to break, conflicts in
prose are rare and obvious when they happen, and the thing you usually want is for everyone
to be reading the same current copy rather than reconciling branches of it later.

A repository can change its mind. Start with a shared checkout and open desks later if the
work turns into code, or the other way round.

Prefer a shared checkout for a repository of documents rather than code — plans, notes,
research, drafts and work in progress. A desk costs ceremony on every edit: a branch to
open, work to commit, a hand-in, a merge. For code that ceremony buys isolation worth
having. For a document it buys almost nothing. There is no build to break, conflicts in
prose are rare and obvious when they happen, and the thing you usually want is for everyone
to be reading the same current copy rather than reconciling branches of it later.

A repository can change its mind. Start with a shared checkout and open desks later if the
work turns into code, or the other way round.

open, work to commit, a hand-in, a merge. For code that ceremony buys isolation worth
having. For a document it buys almost nothing. There is no build to break, conflicts in
prose are rare and obvious when they happen, and the thing you usually want is for everyone
to be reading the same current copy rather than reconciling branches of it later.

A repository can change its mind. Start with a shared checkout and open desks later if the
work turns into code, or the other way round.

hPrefer desks whenever the work is code and more than one Agent may touch it. Parallel
Agents on one checkout share a single set of uncommitted changes, so one Agent's
half-finished edit is visible to every other and easy to lose.

prose are rare and obvious when they happen, and the thing you usually want is for everyone
to be reading the same current copy rather than reconciling branches of it later.

A repository can change its mind. Start with a shared checkout and open desks later if the
work turns into code, or the other way round.

pPrefer desks whenever the work is code and more than one Agent may touch it. Parallel
Agents on one checkout share a single set of uncommitted changes, so one Agent's
half-finished edit is visible to every other and easy to lose.

ePrefer desks whenever the work is code and more than one Agent may touch it. Parallel
Agents on one checkout share a single set of uncommitted changes, so one Agent's
half-finished edit is visible to every other and easy to lose.

Prefer a shared checkout for a repository of documents rather than code — plans, notes,
research, drafts and work in progress. A desk costs ceremony on every edit: a branch to
open, work to commit, a hand-in, a merge. For code that ceremony buys isolation worth
having. For a document it buys almost nothing. There is no build to break, conflicts in
prose are rare and obvious when they happen, and the thing you usually want is for everyone
to be reading the same current copy rather than reconciling branches of it later.

A repository can change its mind. Start with a shared checkout and open desks later if the
work turns into code, or the other way round.

half-finished edit is visible to every other and easy to lose.

Prefer a shared checkout for a repository of documents rather than code — plans, notes,
research, drafts and work in progress. A desk costs ceremony on every edit: a branch to
open, work to commit, a hand-in, a merge. For code that ceremony buys isolation worth
having. For a document it buys almost nothing. There is no build to break, conflicts in
prose are rare and obvious when they happen, and the thing you usually want is for everyone
to be reading the same current copy rather than reconciling branches of it later.

A repository can change its mind. Start with a shared checkout and open desks later if the
work turns into code, or the other way round.

research, drafts and work in progress. A desk costs ceremony on every edit: a branch to
open, work to commit, a hand-in, a merge. For code that ceremony buys isolation worth
having. For a document it buys almost nothing. There is no build to break, conflicts in
prose are rare and obvious when they happen, and the thing you usually want is for everyone
to be reading the same current copy rather than reconciling branches of it later.

A repository can change its mind. Start with a shared checkout and open desks later if the
work turns into code, or the other way round.

having. For a document it buys almost nothing. There is no build to break, conflicts in
prose are rare and obvious when they happen, and the thing you usually want is for everyone
to be reading the same current copy rather than reconciling branches of it later.

A repository can change its mind. Start with a shared checkout and open desks later if the
work turns into code, or the other way round.

 Prefer desks whenever the work is code and more than one Agent may touch it. Parallel
Agents on one checkout share a single set of uncommitted changes, so one Agent's
half-finished edit is visible to every other and easy to lose.

half-finished edit is visible to every other and easy to lose.

Prefer a shared checkout for a repository of documents rather than code — plans, notes,
research, drafts and work in progress. A desk costs ceremony on every edit: a branch to
open, work to commit, a hand-in, a merge. For code that ceremony buys isolation worth
having. For a document it buys almost nothing. There is no build to break, conflicts in
prose are rare and obvious when they happen, and the thing you usually want is for everyone
to be reading the same current copy rather than reconciling branches of it later.

A repository can change its mind. Start with a shared checkout and open desks later if the
work turns into code, or the other way round.

Agents on one checkout share a single set of uncommitted changes, so one Agent's
half-finished edit is visible to every other and easy to lose.

research, drafts and work in progress. A desk costs ceremony on every edit: a branch to
open, work to commit, a hand-in, a merge. For code that ceremony buys isolation worth
having. For a document it buys almost nothing. There is no build to break, conflicts in
prose are rare and obvious when they happen, and the thing you usually want is for everyone
to be reading the same current copy rather than reconciling branches of it later.

A repository can change its mind. Start with a shared checkout and open desks later if the
work turns into code, or the other way round.

dPrefer desks whenever the work is code and more than one Agent may touch it. Parallel
Agents on one checkout share a single set of uncommitted changes, so one Agent's
half-finished edit is visible to every other and easy to lose.

having. For a document it buys almost nothing. There is no build to break, conflicts in
prose are rare and obvious when they happen, and the thing you usually want is for everyone
to be reading the same current copy rather than reconciling branches of it later.

A repository can change its mind. Start with a shared checkout and open desks later if the
work turns into code, or the other way round.

fPrefer desks whenever the work is code and more than one Agent may touch it. Parallel
Agents on one checkout share a single set of uncommitted changes, so one Agent's
half-finished edit is visible to every other and easy to lose.

Agents on one checkout share a single set of uncommitted changes, so one Agent's
half-finished edit is visible to every other and easy to lose.

Prefer a shared checkout for a repository of documents rather than code — plans, notes,
research, drafts and work in progress. A desk costs ceremony on every edit: a branch to
open, work to commit, a hand-in, a merge. For code that ceremony buys isolation worth
having. For a document it buys almost nothing. There is no build to break, conflicts in
prose are rare and obvious when they happen, and the thing you usually want is for everyone
to be reading the same current copy rather than reconciling branches of it later.

A repository can change its mind. Start with a shared checkout and open desks later if the
work turns into code, or the other way round.

research, drafts and work in progress. A desk costs ceremony on every edit: a branch to
open, work to commit, a hand-in, a merge. For code that ceremony buys isolation worth
having. For a document it buys almost nothing. There is no build to break, conflicts in
prose are rare and obvious when they happen, and the thing you usually want is for everyone
to be reading the same current copy rather than reconciling branches of it later.

A repository can change its mind. Start with a shared checkout and open desks later if the
work turns into code, or the other way round.

having. For a document it buys almost nothing. There is no build to break, conflicts in
prose are rare and obvious when they happen, and the thing you usually want is for everyone
to be reading the same current copy rather than reconciling branches of it later.

A repository can change its mind. Start with a shared checkout and open desks later if the
work turns into code, or the other way round.


Prefer desks whenever the work is code and more than one Agent may touch it. Parallel
Agents on one checkout share a single set of uncommitted changes, so one Agent's
half-finished edit is visible to every other and easy to lose.

Agents on one checkout share a single set of uncommitted changes, so one Agent's
half-finished edit is visible to every other and easy to lose.

Prefer a shared checkout for a repository of documents rather than code — plans, notes,
research, drafts and work in progress. A desk costs ceremony on every edit: a branch to
open, work to commit, a hand-in, a merge. For code that ceremony buys isolation worth
having. For a document it buys almost nothing. There is no build to break, conflicts in
prose are rare and obvious when they happen, and the thing you usually want is for everyone
to be reading the same current copy rather than reconciling branches of it later.

A repository can change its mind. Start with a shared checkout and open desks later if the
work turns into code, or the other way round.

Prefer a shared checkout for a repository of documents rather than code — plans, notes,
research, drafts and work in progress. A desk costs ceremony on every edit: a branch to
open, work to commit, a hand-in, a merge. For code that ceremony buys isolation worth
having. For a document it buys almost nothing. There is no build to break, conflicts in
prose are rare and obvious when they happen, and the thing you usually want is for everyone
to be reading the same current copy rather than reconciling branches of it later.

A repository can change its mind. Start with a shared checkout and open desks later if the
work turns into code, or the other way round.

open, work to commit, a hand-in, a merge. For code that ceremony buys isolation worth
having. For a document it buys almost nothing. There is no build to break, conflicts in
prose are rare and obvious when they happen, and the thing you usually want is for everyone
to be reading the same current copy rather than reconciling branches of it later.

A repository can change its mind. Start with a shared checkout and open desks later if the
work turns into code, or the other way round.

nPrefer desks whenever the work is code and more than one Agent may touch it. Parallel
Agents on one checkout share a single set of uncommitted changes, so one Agent's
half-finished edit is visible to every other and easy to lose.

prose are rare and obvious when they happen, and the thing you usually want is for everyone
to be reading the same current copy rather than reconciling branches of it later.

A repository can change its mind. Start with a shared checkout and open desks later if the
work turns into code, or the other way round.

ePrefer desks whenever the work is code and more than one Agent may touch it. Parallel
Agents on one checkout share a single set of uncommitted changes, so one Agent's
half-finished edit is visible to every other and easy to lose.

 Prefer desks whenever the work is code and more than one Agent may touch it. Parallel
Agents on one checkout share a single set of uncommitted changes, so one Agent's
half-finished edit is visible to every other and easy to lose.

Prefer a shared checkout for a repository of documents rather than code — plans, notes,
research, drafts and work in progress. A desk costs ceremony on every edit: a branch to
open, work to commit, a hand-in, a merge. For code that ceremony buys isolation worth
having. For a document it buys almost nothing. There is no build to break, conflicts in
prose are rare and obvious when they happen, and the thing you usually want is for everyone
to be reading the same current copy rather than reconciling branches of it later.

work turns into code, or the other way round.

Prefer a shared checkout for a repository of documents rather than code — plans, notes,
research, drafts and work in progress. A desk costs ceremony on every edit: a branch to
open, work to commit, a hand-in, a merge. For code that ceremony buys isolation worth
having. For a document it buys almost nothing. There is no build to break, conflicts in
prose are rare and obvious when they happen, and the thing you usually want is for everyone
to be reading the same current copy rather than reconciling branches of it later.

A repository can change its mind. Start with a shared checkout and open desks later if the
work turns into code, or the other way round.

open, work to commit, a hand-in, a merge. For code that ceremony buys isolation worth
having. For a document it buys almost nothing. There is no build to break, conflicts in
prose are rare and obvious when they happen, and the thing you usually want is for everyone
to be reading the same current copy rather than reconciling branches of it later.

A repository can change its mind. Start with a shared checkout and open desks later if the
work turns into code, or the other way round.

 Prefer desks whenever the work is code and more than one Agent may touch it. Parallel
Agents on one checkout share a single set of uncommitted changes, so one Agent's
half-finished edit is visible to every other and easy to lose.

prose are rare and obvious when they happen, and the thing you usually want is for everyone
to be reading the same current copy rather than reconciling branches of it later.

A repository can change its mind. Start with a shared checkout and open desks later if the
work turns into code, or the other way round.

tPrefer desks whenever the work is code and more than one Agent may touch it. Parallel
Agents on one checkout share a single set of uncommitted changes, so one Agent's
half-finished edit is visible to every other and easy to lose.

iPrefer desks whenever the work is code and more than one Agent may touch it. Parallel
Agents on one checkout share a single set of uncommitted changes, so one Agent's
half-finished edit is visible to every other and easy to lose.

Prefer a shared checkout for a repository of documents rather than code — plans, notes,
research, drafts and work in progress. A desk costs ceremony on every edit: a branch to
open, work to commit, a hand-in, a merge. For code that ceremony buys isolation worth
having. For a document it buys almost nothing. There is no build to break, conflicts in
prose are rare and obvious when they happen, and the thing you usually want is for everyone
to be reading the same current copy rather than reconciling branches of it later.

A repository can change its mind. Start with a shared checkout and open desks later if the
work turns into code, or the other way round.

half-finished edit is visible to every other and easy to lose.

Prefer a shared checkout for a repository of documents rather than code — plans, notes,
research, drafts and work in progress. A desk costs ceremony on every edit: a branch to
open, work to commit, a hand-in, a merge. For code that ceremony buys isolation worth
having. For a document it buys almost nothing. There is no build to break, conflicts in
prose are rare and obvious when they happen, and the thing you usually want is for everyone
to be reading the same current copy rather than reconciling branches of it later.

A repository can change its mind. Start with a shared checkout and open desks later if the
work turns into code, or the other way round.

Agents on one checkout share a single set of uncommitted changes, so one Agent's
half-finished edit is visible to every other and easy to lose.

research, drafts and work in progress. A desk costs ceremony on every edit: a branch to
open, work to commit, a hand-in, a merge. For code that ceremony buys isolation worth
having. For a document it buys almost nothing. There is no build to break, conflicts in
prose are rare and obvious when they happen, and the thing you usually want is for everyone
to be reading the same current copy rather than reconciling branches of it later.

A repository can change its mind. Start with a shared checkout and open desks later if the
work turns into code, or the other way round.

Agents on one checkout share a single set of uncommitted changes, so one Agent's
half-finished edit is visible to every other and easy to lose.

having. For a document it buys almost nothing. There is no build to break, conflicts in
prose are rare and obvious when they happen, and the thing you usually want is for everyone
to be reading the same current copy rather than reconciling branches of it later.

A repository can change its mind. Start with a shared checkout and open desks later if the
work turns into code, or the other way round.

rPrefer desks whenever the work is code and more than one Agent may touch it. Parallel
Agents on one checkout share a single set of uncommitted changes, so one Agent's
half-finished edit is visible to every other and easy to lose.

Agents on one checkout share a single set of uncommitted changes, so one Agent's
half-finished edit is visible to every other and easy to lose.

Prefer a shared checkout for a repository of documents rather than code — plans, notes,
research, drafts and work in progress. A desk costs ceremony on every edit: a branch to
open, work to commit, a hand-in, a merge. For code that ceremony buys isolation worth
having. For a document it buys almost nothing. There is no build to break, conflicts in
prose are rare and obvious when they happen, and the thing you usually want is for everyone
to be reading the same current copy rather than reconciling branches of it later.

A repository can change its mind. Start with a shared checkout and open desks later if the
work turns into code, or the other way round.

research, drafts and work in progress. A desk costs ceremony on every edit: a branch to
open, work to commit, a hand-in, a merge. For code that ceremony buys isolation worth
having. For a document it buys almost nothing. There is no build to break, conflicts in
prose are rare and obvious when they happen, and the thing you usually want is for everyone
to be reading the same current copy rather than reconciling branches of it later.

A repository can change its mind. Start with a shared checkout and open desks later if the
work turns into code, or the other way round.

ePrefer desks whenever the work is code and more than one Agent may touch it. Parallel
Agents on one checkout share a single set of uncommitted changes, so one Agent's
half-finished edit is visible to every other and easy to lose.

having. For a document it buys almost nothing. There is no build to break, conflicts in
prose are rare and obvious when they happen, and the thing you usually want is for everyone
to be reading the same current copy rather than reconciling branches of it later.

A repository can change its mind. Start with a shared checkout and open desks later if the
work turns into code, or the other way round.

Agents on one checkout share a single set of uncommitted changes, so one Agent's

Agents on one checkout share a single set of uncommitted changes, so one Agent's
half-finished edit is visible to every other and easy to lose.

Prefer a shared checkout for a repository of documents rather than code — plans, notes,
research, drafts and work in progress. A desk costs ceremony on every edit: a branch to
open, work to commit, a hand-in, a merge. For code that ceremony buys isolation worth
having. For a document it buys almost nothing. There is no build to break, conflicts in
prose are rare and obvious when they happen, and the thing you usually want is for everyone
to be reading the same current copy rather than reconciling branches of it later.

A repository can change its mind. Start with a shared checkout and open desks later if the
work turns into code, or the other way round.

half-finished edit is visible to every other and easy to lose.

having. For a document it buys almost nothing. There is no build to break, conflicts in
prose are rare and obvious when they happen, and the thing you usually want is for everyone
to be reading the same current copy rather than reconciling branches of it later.

A repository can change its mind. Start with a shared checkout and open desks later if the
work turns into code, or the other way round.

rPrefer desks whenever the work is code and more than one Agent may touch it. Parallel
Agents on one checkout share a single set of uncommitted changes, so one Agent's
half-finished edit is visible to every other and easy to lose.

Agents on one checkout share a single set of uncommitted changes, so one Agent's
half-finished edit is visible to every other and easy to lose.

Prefer a shared checkout for a repository of documents rather than code — plans, notes,
research, drafts and work in progress. A desk costs ceremony on every edit: a branch to
open, work to commit, a hand-in, a merge. For code that ceremony buys isolation worth
having. For a document it buys almost nothing. There is no build to break, conflicts in
prose are rare and obvious when they happen, and the thing you usually want is for everyone
to be reading the same current copy rather than reconciling branches of it later.

A repository can change its mind. Start with a shared checkout and open desks later if the
work turns into code, or the other way round.

research, drafts and work in progress. A desk costs ceremony on every edit: a branch to
open, work to commit, a hand-in, a merge. For code that ceremony buys isolation worth
having. For a document it buys almost nothing. There is no build to break, conflicts in
prose are rare and obvious when they happen, and the thing you usually want is for everyone
to be reading the same current copy rather than reconciling branches of it later.

A repository can change its mind. Start with a shared checkout and open desks later if the
work turns into code, or the other way round.

oPrefer desks whenever the work is code and more than one Agent may touch it. Parallel
Agents on one checkout share a single set of uncommitted changes, so one Agent's
half-finished edit is visible to every other and easy to lose.

having. For a document it buys almost nothing. There is no build to break, conflicts in
prose are rare and obvious when they happen, and the thing you usually want is for everyone
to be reading the same current copy rather than reconciling branches of it later.

A repository can change its mind. Start with a shared checkout and open desks later if the
work turns into code, or the other way round.

Agents on one checkout share a single set of uncommitted changes, so one Agent's
half-finished edit is visible to every other and easy to lose.

Prefer a shared checkout for a repository of documents rather than code — plans, notes,
research, drafts and work in progress. A desk costs ceremony on every edit: a branch to
open, work to commit, a hand-in, a merge. For code that ceremony buys isolation worth
having. For a document it buys almost nothing. There is no build to break, conflicts in
prose are rare and obvious when they happen, and the thing you usually want is for everyone
to be reading the same current copy rather than reconciling branches of it later.

A repository can change its mind. Start with a shared checkout and open desks later if the
work turns into code, or the other way round.

research, drafts and work in progress. A desk costs ceremony on every edit: a branch to
open, work to commit, a hand-in, a merge. For code that ceremony buys isolation worth
having. For a document it buys almost nothing. There is no build to break, conflicts in
prose are rare and obvious when they happen, and the thing you usually want is for everyone
to be reading the same current copy rather than reconciling branches of it later.

A repository can change its mind. Start with a shared checkout and open desks later if the
work turns into code, or the other way round.

ePrefer desks whenever the work is code and more than one Agent may touch it. Parallel
Agents on one checkout share a single set of uncommitted changes, so one Agent's
half-finished edit is visible to every other and easy to lose.

having. For a document it buys almost nothing. There is no build to break, conflicts in
prose are rare and obvious when they happen, and the thing you usually want is for everyone
to be reading the same current copy rather than reconciling branches of it later.

A repository can change its mind. Start with a shared checkout and open desks later if the
work turns into code, or the other way round.

aPrefer desks whenever the work is code and more than one Agent may touch it. Parallel
Agents on one checkout share a single set of uncommitted changes, so one Agent's
half-finished edit is visible to every other and easy to lose.

Agents on one checkout share a single set of uncommitted changes, so one Agent's
half-finished edit is visible to every other and easy to lose.

Prefer a shared checkout for a repository of documents rather than code — plans, notes,
research, drafts and work in progress. A desk costs ceremony on every edit: a branch to
open, work to commit, a hand-in, a merge. For code that ceremony buys isolation worth
having. For a document it buys almost nothing. There is no build to break, conflicts in
prose are rare and obvious when they happen, and the thing you usually want is for everyone
to be reading the same current copy rather than reconciling branches of it later.

A repository can change its mind. Start with a shared checkout and open desks later if the
work turns into code, or the other way round.

research, drafts and work in progress. A desk costs ceremony on every edit: a branch to
open, work to commit, a hand-in, a merge. For code that ceremony buys isolation worth
having. For a document it buys almost nothing. There is no build to break, conflicts in
prose are rare and obvious when they happen, and the thing you usually want is for everyone
to be reading the same current copy rather than reconciling branches of it later.

A repository can change its mind. Start with a shared checkout and open desks later if the
work turns into code, or the other way round.

having. For a document it buys almost nothing. There is no build to break, conflicts in
prose are rare and obvious when they happen, and the thing you usually want is for everyone
to be reading the same current copy rather than reconciling branches of it later.

A repository can change its mind. Start with a shared checkout and open desks later if the
work turns into code, or the other way round.

pPrefer desks whenever the work is code and more than one Agent may touch it. Parallel
Agents on one checkout share a single set of uncommitted changes, so one Agent's
half-finished edit is visible to every other and easy to lose.

sPrefer desks whenever the work is code and more than one Agent may touch it. Parallel
Agents on one checkout share a single set of uncommitted changes, so one Agent's
half-finished edit is visible to every other and easy to lose.

Prefer a shared checkout for a repository of documents rather than code — plans, notes,
research, drafts and work in progress. A desk costs ceremony on every edit: a branch to
open, work to commit, a hand-in, a merge. For code that ceremony buys isolation worth
having. For a document it buys almost nothing. There is no build to break, conflicts in
prose are rare and obvious when they happen, and the thing you usually want is for everyone
to be reading the same current copy rather than reconciling branches of it later.

A repository can change its mind. Start with a shared checkout and open desks later if the
work turns into code, or the other way round.

Prefer a shared checkout for a repository of documents rather than code — plans, notes,
research, drafts and work in progress. A desk costs ceremony on every edit: a branch to
open, work to commit, a hand-in, a merge. For code that ceremony buys isolation worth
having. For a document it buys almost nothing. There is no build to break, conflicts in
prose are rare and obvious when they happen, and the thing you usually want is for everyone
to be reading the same current copy rather than reconciling branches of it later.

A repository can change its mind. Start with a shared checkout and open desks later if the
work turns into code, or the other way round.

open, work to commit, a hand-in, a merge. For code that ceremony buys isolation worth
having. For a document it buys almost nothing. There is no build to break, conflicts in
prose are rare and obvious when they happen, and the thing you usually want is for everyone
to be reading the same current copy rather than reconciling branches of it later.

A repository can change its mind. Start with a shared checkout and open desks later if the
work turns into code, or the other way round.

yPrefer desks whenever the work is code and more than one Agent may touch it. Parallel
Agents on one checkout share a single set of uncommitted changes, so one Agent's
half-finished edit is visible to every other and easy to lose.

work turns into code, or the other way round.

Agents on one checkout share a single set of uncommitted changes, so one Agent's
half-finished edit is visible to every other and easy to lose.

Prefer a shared checkout for a repository of documents rather than code — plans, notes,
research, drafts and work in progress. A desk costs ceremony on every edit: a branch to
open, work to commit, a hand-in, a merge. For code that ceremony buys isolation worth
having. For a document it buys almost nothing. There is no build to break, conflicts in
prose are rare and obvious when they happen, and the thing you usually want is for everyone
to be reading the same current copy rather than reconciling branches of it later.

A repository can change its mind. Start with a shared checkout and open desks later if the
work turns into code, or the other way round.

ePrefer desks whenever the work is code and more than one Agent may touch it. Parallel
Agents on one checkout share a single set of uncommitted changes, so one Agent's
half-finished edit is visible to every other and easy to lose.

research, drafts and work in progress. A desk costs ceremony on every edit: a branch to
open, work to commit, a hand-in, a merge. For code that ceremony buys isolation worth
having. For a document it buys almost nothing. There is no build to break, conflicts in
prose are rare and obvious when they happen, and the thing you usually want is for everyone
to be reading the same current copy rather than reconciling branches of it later.

work turns into code, or the other way round.

having. For a document it buys almost nothing. There is no build to break, conflicts in
prose are rare and obvious when they happen, and the thing you usually want is for everyone
to be reading the same current copy rather than reconciling branches of it later.

A repository can change its mind. Start with a shared checkout and open desks later if the
work turns into code, or the other way round.

ePrefer desks whenever the work is code and more than one Agent may touch it. Parallel
Agents on one checkout share a single set of uncommitted changes, so one Agent's
half-finished edit is visible to every other and easy to lose.

Agents on one checkout share a single set of uncommitted changes, so one Agent's
half-finished edit is visible to every other and easy to lose.

Prefer a shared checkout for a repository of documents rather than code — plans, notes,
research, drafts and work in progress. A desk costs ceremony on every edit: a branch to
open, work to commit, a hand-in, a merge. For code that ceremony buys isolation worth
having. For a document it buys almost nothing. There is no build to break, conflicts in
prose are rare and obvious when they happen, and the thing you usually want is for everyone
to be reading the same current copy rather than reconciling branches of it later.

A repository can change its mind. Start with a shared checkout and open desks later if the
work turns into code, or the other way round.

ePrefer desks whenever the work is code and more than one Agent may touch it. Parallel
Agents on one checkout share a single set of uncommitted changes, so one Agent's
half-finished edit is visible to every other and easy to lose.

Prefer a shared checkout for a repository of documents rather than code — plans, notes,
research, drafts and work in progress. A desk costs ceremony on every edit: a branch to
open, work to commit, a hand-in, a merge. For code that ceremony buys isolation worth
having. For a document it buys almost nothing. There is no build to break, conflicts in
prose are rare and obvious when they happen, and the thing you usually want is for everyone
to be reading the same current copy rather than reconciling branches of it later.

A repository can change its mind. Start with a shared checkout and open desks later if the
work turns into code, or the other way round.

open, work to commit, a hand-in, a merge. For code that ceremony buys isolation worth
having. For a document it buys almost nothing. There is no build to break, conflicts in
prose are rare and obvious when they happen, and the thing you usually want is for everyone
to be reading the same current copy rather than reconciling branches of it later.

A repository can change its mind. Start with a shared checkout and open desks later if the
work turns into code, or the other way round.

,Prefer desks whenever the work is code and more than one Agent may touch it. Parallel
Agents on one checkout share a single set of uncommitted changes, so one Agent's
half-finished edit is visible to every other and easy to lose.

prose are rare and obvious when they happen, and the thing you usually want is for everyone
to be reading the same current copy rather than reconciling branches of it later.

A repository can change its mind. Start with a shared checkout and open desks later if the
work turns into code, or the other way round.

vPrefer desks whenever the work is code and more than one Agent may touch it. Parallel
Agents on one checkout share a single set of uncommitted changes, so one Agent's
half-finished edit is visible to every other and easy to lose.

uPrefer desks whenever the work is code and more than one Agent may touch it. Parallel
Agents on one checkout share a single set of uncommitted changes, so one Agent's
half-finished edit is visible to every other and easy to lose.

Prefer a shared checkout for a repository of documents rather than code — plans, notes,
research, drafts and work in progress. A desk costs ceremony on every edit: a branch to
open, work to commit, a hand-in, a merge. For code that ceremony buys isolation worth
having. For a document it buys almost nothing. There is no build to break, conflicts in
prose are rare and obvious when they happen, and the thing you usually want is for everyone
to be reading the same current copy rather than reconciling branches of it later.

A repository can change its mind. Start with a shared checkout and open desks later if the
work turns into code, or the other way round.

Prefer a shared checkout for a repository of documents rather than code — plans, notes,
research, drafts and work in progress. A desk costs ceremony on every edit: a branch to
open, work to commit, a hand-in, a merge. For code that ceremony buys isolation worth
having. For a document it buys almost nothing. There is no build to break, conflicts in
prose are rare and obvious when they happen, and the thing you usually want is for everyone
to be reading the same current copy rather than reconciling branches of it later.

A repository can change its mind. Start with a shared checkout and open desks later if the
work turns into code, or the other way round.

open, work to commit, a hand-in, a merge. For code that ceremony buys isolation worth
having. For a document it buys almost nothing. There is no build to break, conflicts in
prose are rare and obvious when they happen, and the thing you usually want is for everyone
to be reading the same current copy rather than reconciling branches of it later.

A repository can change its mind. Start with a shared checkout and open desks later if the
work turns into code, or the other way round.

 Prefer desks whenever the work is code and more than one Agent may touch it. Parallel
Agents on one checkout share a single set of uncommitted changes, so one Agent's
half-finished edit is visible to every other and easy to lose.

prose are rare and obvious when they happen, and the thing you usually want is for everyone
to be reading the same current copy rather than reconciling branches of it later.

A repository can change its mind. Start with a shared checkout and open desks later if the
work turns into code, or the other way round.

oPrefer desks whenever the work is code and more than one Agent may touch it. Parallel
Agents on one checkout share a single set of uncommitted changes, so one Agent's
half-finished edit is visible to every other and easy to lose.

 Prefer desks whenever the work is code and more than one Agent may touch it. Parallel
Agents on one checkout share a single set of uncommitted changes, so one Agent's
half-finished edit is visible to every other and easy to lose.

Prefer a shared checkout for a repository of documents rather than code — plans, notes,
research, drafts and work in progress. A desk costs ceremony on every edit: a branch to
open, work to commit, a hand-in, a merge. For code that ceremony buys isolation worth
having. For a document it buys almost nothing. There is no build to break, conflicts in
prose are rare and obvious when they happen, and the thing you usually want is for everyone
to be reading the same current copy rather than reconciling branches of it later.

A repository can change its mind. Start with a shared checkout and open desks later if the
work turns into code, or the other way round.

half-finished edit is visible to every other and easy to lose.

Prefer a shared checkout for a repository of documents rather than code — plans, notes,
research, drafts and work in progress. A desk costs ceremony on every edit: a branch to
open, work to commit, a hand-in, a merge. For code that ceremony buys isolation worth
having. For a document it buys almost nothing. There is no build to break, conflicts in
prose are rare and obvious when they happen, and the thing you usually want is for everyone
to be reading the same current copy rather than reconciling branches of it later.

A repository can change its mind. Start with a shared checkout and open desks later if the
work turns into code, or the other way round.

research, drafts and work in progress. A desk costs ceremony on every edit: a branch to
open, work to commit, a hand-in, a merge. For code that ceremony buys isolation worth
having. For a document it buys almost nothing. There is no build to break, conflicts in
prose are rare and obvious when they happen, and the thing you usually want is for everyone
to be reading the same current copy rather than reconciling branches of it later.

A repository can change its mind. Start with a shared checkout and open desks later if the
work turns into code, or the other way round.

lPrefer desks whenever the work is code and more than one Agent may touch it. Parallel
Agents on one checkout share a single set of uncommitted changes, so one Agent's
half-finished edit is visible to every other and easy to lose.

having. For a document it buys almost nothing. There is no build to break, conflicts in
prose are rare and obvious when they happen, and the thing you usually want is for everyone
to be reading the same current copy rather than reconciling branches of it later.

A repository can change its mind. Start with a shared checkout and open desks later if the
work turns into code, or the other way round.

hPrefer desks whenever the work is code and more than one Agent may touch it. Parallel
Agents on one checkout share a single set of uncommitted changes, so one Agent's
half-finished edit is visible to every other and easy to lose.

Agents on one checkout share a single set of uncommitted changes, so one Agent's
half-finished edit is visible to every other and easy to lose.

Prefer a shared checkout for a repository of documents rather than code — plans, notes,
research, drafts and work in progress. A desk costs ceremony on every edit: a branch to
open, work to commit, a hand-in, a merge. For code that ceremony buys isolation worth
having. For a document it buys almost nothing. There is no build to break, conflicts in
prose are rare and obvious when they happen, and the thing you usually want is for everyone
to be reading the same current copy rather than reconciling branches of it later.

A repository can change its mind. Start with a shared checkout and open desks later if the
work turns into code, or the other way round.

Agents on one checkout share a single set of uncommitted changes, so one Agent's

research, drafts and work in progress. A desk costs ceremony on every edit: a branch to
open, work to commit, a hand-in, a merge. For code that ceremony buys isolation worth
having. For a document it buys almost nothing. There is no build to break, conflicts in
prose are rare and obvious when they happen, and the thing you usually want is for everyone
to be reading the same current copy rather than reconciling branches of it later.

A repository can change its mind. Start with a shared checkout and open desks later if the
work turns into code, or the other way round.

sPrefer desks whenever the work is code and more than one Agent may touch it. Parallel
Agents on one checkout share a single set of uncommitted changes, so one Agent's
half-finished edit is visible to every other and easy to lose.

having. For a document it buys almost nothing. There is no build to break, conflicts in
prose are rare and obvious when they happen, and the thing you usually want is for everyone
to be reading the same current copy rather than reconciling branches of it later.

A repository can change its mind. Start with a shared checkout and open desks later if the
work turns into code, or the other way round.

iPrefer desks whenever the work is code and more than one Agent may touch it. Parallel
Agents on one checkout share a single set of uncommitted changes, so one Agent's
half-finished edit is visible to every other and easy to lose.

nPrefer desks whenever the work is code and more than one Agent may touch it. Parallel
Agents on one checkout share a single set of uncommitted changes, so one Agent's
half-finished edit is visible to every other and easy to lose.

Prefer a shared checkout for a repository of documents rather than code — plans, notes,
research, drafts and work in progress. A desk costs ceremony on every edit: a branch to
open, work to commit, a hand-in, a merge. For code that ceremony buys isolation worth
having. For a document it buys almost nothing. There is no build to break, conflicts in
prose are rare and obvious when they happen, and the thing you usually want is for everyone
to be reading the same current copy rather than reconciling branches of it later.

A repository can change its mind. Start with a shared checkout and open desks later if the
work turns into code, or the other way round.
